summary:
Round-7 delta verified BY MEASUREMENT in an isolated review tree (254-test sequencer suite; full ./gradlew test green unmutated). The new derived assertion in aKeyTooSHORTToCarryTheGrammarIsRefusedRatherThanThrowing does exactly what round 6 asked: it is the SOLE killer, among the five assertions of that method, of all three prefix-guard narrowings -- trailing '/' dropped, epoch segment dropped, and startsWith replaced by a bare length test (round 4's T5 survivor). Measured by isolating each assertion in turn. mutants.txt entry 3 is gone and the two remaining entries are true survivors of the FULL suite, re-measured. Every ChainReplay filter mutant an earlier round measured still dies, including the I3 swallowing form and all three acceptance-criteria-named alternative filters. No assertion weakened; check-test-integrity and check-tdd both ok. One minor, not blocking: the `contains(SUFFIX)` entry's own final sentence names a reachable input on which the mutant throws, and a four-line probe kills it -- measured.

ANSWERS TO THE QUESTIONS ASKED, each measured in an isolated review tree:

[T2] Answering the two questions asked: the new assertion's unique kills, and whether `bins.delta` should now be DELETED (recommendation: KEEP) (sequencer/src/test/java/binjava/sequencer/LogKeysTest.java:82)
PER-ASSERTION KILL MATRIX for aKeyTooSHORTToCarryTheGrammarIsRefusedRatherThanThrowing, measured by commenting out four of the five assertions at a time and re-running the class against each mutant (A1=".delta", A2=logPrefix()+"x", A3="bins.delta", A4=the new derived proper-prefix key, A5=logPrefix()+"delta"):

  startsWith(logPrefix) -> startsWith(logPrefix minus trailing '/')  : killed by A4 ONLY
  startsWith(logPrefix) -> startsWith(prefix + "/ctl/log/0/")         : killed by A4 ONLY
  startsWith(logPrefix) -> key.length() < logPrefix.length()          : killed by A4 ONLY
  startsWith(logPrefix) -> startsWith(prefix)                         : killed by A3 and A4
  startsWith guard deleted                                            : killed by A1, A3, A4
  endsWith guard deleted                                             : killed by A2 and A5
  endsWith(SUFFIX) -> endsWith("delta")                              : killed by A5 ONLY
  ||  ->  &&                                                          : killed by A2

So A4 is the sole killer of three mutants and passes unmutated -- the author's measurement reproduces exactly. A5 is the sole killer of one. A1, A2 and A3 are each STRICTLY SUBSUMED by A4 or A5 over this mutant set; A3's kills are a proper subset of A4's, as I said last round.

DELETE OR KEEP A3? KEEP. Deleting buys one line and loses the only case whose shape names the record component, and non-negotiable 2 is not the operative rule here (nothing is being made to pass) but its habit is the right one at round 7. The more useful observation is the direction of durability, which runs OPPOSITE to the redundancy: A3 hardcodes "bins", so if the log-prefix grammar ever stopped starting with the prefix component, A3 would silently become vacuous -- it would return false at the first guard for a trivial reason -- while A4, deriving from logPrefix(), would follow the grammar. If one of the five is ever dropped, drop A1 (`.delta`), which kills only what A3 and A4 both already kill.

Same conclusion for A1 and A2: subsumed, harmless, each documents a distinct grammar case with a self-explaining .as(). Not a finding.

[T3] Deriving the key from KEYS.logPrefix() rather than hardcoding it does NOT weaken the assertion -- measured, including the case where it might have (sequencer/src/test/java/binjava/sequencer/LogKeysTest.java:88)
The theoretical cost of deriving is that a mutation of logPrefix() itself rewrites the test's INPUT and the assertion goes vacuous. I mutated logPrefix()'s format string two ways to check whether anything catches such a change:

  "%s/ctl/log/0/%016x/" -> "%s/ctl/log/0/%016x"  (trailing slash dropped) : killed by CommitLogTest.theKeyCarriesTheEpochZeroPaddedSoLexicographicOrderIsNumericOrder
  "%s/ctl/log/0/%016x/" -> "%s/ctl/log/0/"       (epoch segment dropped)  : killed by the same test plus ~10 others
  keyFor's "%016x" -> "%08x"                                            : killed by the same test

That test asserts the grammar against a STRING LITERAL, so the grammar cannot drift under A4 without a loud failure elsewhere. A4 is therefore free to derive.

AND THE HARDCODED FORM WOULD NOT HAVE BEEN STRONGER HERE ANYWAY, which I did not realise when I proposed it: under the trailing-slash mutation of logPrefix(), the literal "bins/ctl/log/0/0000000000000001.delta" passes both guards, slices digits = substring(31, 31) = "", hits NumberFormatException and returns false -- so the literal assertion passes silently too. The two forms are equally strong on this axis, and the derived one is consistent with the rest of the file (KEYS.keyFor(0), p + "9.delta").

[T4] Round 4's other two T5 survivors are still survivors, and both are PROVABLY equivalent -- leaving them unargued is not a rule-9 gap (baselines/mutants.txt:56)
Re-measured on the staged bytes; both survive the whole sequencer suite. Both are equivalent on the return value, by proof rather than by absence of a failing test:

  catch (NumberFormatException) { sequence = 0; }  -- falls through to key.equals(keyFor(0)). Every key reaching the catch has digits that FAILED hex parsing; keyFor(0)'s digits are "0000000000000000", which parse. So key can never equal keyFor(0), and the result is false either way.

  both guards -> if (key.length() < logPrefix.length() + SUFFIX.length()) return false;  -- the canonical equals is the only route to true, and the length precondition makes the substring total, so the return value is identical for every input. The mutant is STRICTLY SAFER: it cannot throw where production can.

Neither is produced by a standard mutation operator (PIT has nothing that rewrites two String predicates into a length comparison, or a return-in-catch into an assignment), so check-mutants.sh when it lands would not report them. Contrast the third T5 survivor, `startsWith -> length test`, which IS a plain conditional replacement and which this delta now KILLS via A4. I would not add entries for these two; if the author prefers belt and braces, one two-line entry covers both.

For completeness, `catch { return true; }` -- which IS a standard operator -- is killed, by LogKeysTest.aKeyThatIsNotThisChainsAtAllIsRefused and ChainReplayNonDeltaKeyTest.aValidEntryAtAKeyThisLogNeverWroteIsNotPartOfItsChain.

[T5] Regression check: every kill earlier rounds measured still holds on the staged bytes, including the I3 swallowing form and all three AC-named alternative filters (sequencer/src/test/java/binjava/sequencer/ChainReplayNonDeltaKeyTest.java:1)
Re-measured, one mutant at a time, whole sequencer suite:

  chainEnd filter continue -> break                : killed by findingTheChainEndIgnoresKeysThatAreNotChainEntries (this is what the .delta.tmp interposed key buys; the trailing ckpt/ key alone would leave it alive)
  chainEnd filter deleted                          : killed by that test + aValidEntryAtAKeyThisLogNeverWroteIsNotPartOfItsChain
  chainEnd predicate negated                       : killed
  applyChain filter continue -> break              : killed by recoveryIgnoresKeysUnderTheLogPrefixThatAreNotChainEntries
  applyChain filter continue -> return             : killed by the same
  applyChain filter deleted / negated              : killed by three of the four
  filter removed and read() wrapped in catch (IOException) { continue; }  (the I3 form)
                                                   : killed by recoveryDoesNotGetNonDeltaKeysAtAllHoweverManyThereAre AND by the pre-existing CommitLogTest.recoveryStopsOnAnEntryItCannotUnderstandRatherThanSkippingIt

And the three alternative filters the acceptance criteria name by hand, substituted for isEntryKey at BOTH sites:

  stat.key().contains(".delta")     : killed by three tests
  deny-list !endsWith(".ckpt")      : killed by three tests
  endsWith(".delta")                : killed by aValidEntryAtAKeyThisLogNeverWroteIsNotPartOfItsChain

The LogKeysTest javadoc's amended claim (item 3 of the delta) is accurate: of the three interlopers ChainReplayNonDeltaKeyTest seeds, .delta.tmp and .ckpt die at the suffix guard and ckpt/<hex>.delta at Long.parseUnsignedLong -- which is why `return true` at the round trip survives that whole class and dies only in LogKeysTest, as I measured again here.

Rules 4-5: both test files are new (git status A), no existing assertion touched; check-test-integrity.sh ok, check-tdd.sh ok (8 new tests, all with red records, unchanged since). Staged diff unchanged at 9a156d61; ./gradlew test green on those exact bytes.

findings.title: The `contains(SUFFIX)` entry is headed EQUIVALENT while its own last sentence names a reachable input that kills it; a measured four-line probe does
findings.failure_scenario: An operator configures a log prefix containing '.delta' (nothing validates prefix beyond Objects.requireNonNull in CommitLog's constructor). If isEntryKey's suffix guard is ever widened to contains(SUFFIX) -- exactly the mutant this baselines/mutants.txt entry declares equivalent and therefore licenses a future author to introduce -- then every LIST page during recovery hits a key under that prefix that is shorter than logPrefix+SUFFIX, isEntryKey throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException instead of returning false, recoverChainEnd propagates it, LocalSequencer.start releases the lease, and the next node repeats forever. That is the identical wedge this whole task exists to fix, re-entered through the argued-equivalent door. No test in the tree would fail: measured, the mutant survives the FULL ./gradlew test today.
